# Abstract

Between 2021 and early 2026, the Russian invasion of Ukraine reduced the combined resident population of Ukraine, Belarus and the Russian Federation (123 administrative and occupation-history divisions covering 17,96M km2) by 9,52M (-4,8%), from 198,08M to 188,56M. Within its 1991 borders, Ukraine's resident population fell by 6,21M (-14,2%) from 43,87M to 37,66M - roughly 31,4M in Kyiv-controlled territory and 6,2M in Russian-occupied territory - alongside 6,4M refugees abroad and 3,67M internally displaced persons, shifting the country's demographic weight from the devastated eastern and southern frontlines toward Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk and the western oblasts. Over the same five years, Belarus declined by 380k (-4,1%, from 9,35M to 8,97M) and the Russian Federation within its 1991 borders by 2,93M (-2%, from 144,86M to 141,93M), as natural decrease, wartime emigration and unequal military casualties fell heaviest on Russia's peripheral ethnic republics and garrison oblasts while largely sparing Moscow and Saint Petersburg.

# Background

Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022 triggered the sharpest demographic and migratory upheaval in Europe since the Second World War [@libanova2023ukraine; @libanova2024demographic; @unhcr2025ukraine; @iom2025returns]. Whereas earlier volumes in this series follow river basins or imperial provinces, wartime demography between 2021 and 2026 is governed by first-level administrative jurisdictions: the 27 constitutional oblasts, autonomous republic and special-status cities of Ukraine, the 7 administrative divisions of Belarus and the 83 internationally recognised federal subjects of the Russian Federation. Across these 123 divisions (17,96M km2; Figure \ref{fig:hero}), the resident population fell by 9,52M (-4,8%), dropping from 198,08M in 2021 to 192,05M after the initial invasion shock in 2022 and reaching 188,56M by early 2026 (Table \ref{tab:macro-summary}).

In Ukraine, the Law *On the Foundations of National Resistance* (Law No. 1702-IX, effective 1 January 2022) and Presidential Decree No. 68/2022 of 24 February 2022 converted every regional administration into an Oblast Military Administration (*Oblasna viiskova administratsiia*) paired with a Territorial Defence Brigade (the 100th to 128th and 241st Brigades) and regional recruitment centres [@ukraine2024strategy; @libanova2023ukraine]. Mandatory frontline evacuations, curfews, fortifications and *eVidnovlennia* housing-reconstruction grants are administered oblast by oblast. Both the Ministry of Social Policy's Unified IDP Database and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) Displacement Tracking Matrix (Rounds 1 to 18+) record Ukraine's 3,67M active internally displaced persons and 4,45M returnees by oblast of origin and current residence, while ACLED conflict logs and the DeepState line of contact map directly onto Ukraine's oblasts and 2020 raions [@iom2022gps; @iom2024displacement; @iom2025returns; @acled2025ukraine; @deepstate2025map]. Where shifting frontlines split an oblast's population history between 2014 and 2026, this study subdivides Donetsk (government-controlled, post-2022 occupied and pre-2022 occupied), Luhansk (post-2022 occupied and pre-2022 occupied), Kharkiv (unoccupied core, 2022 liberated and Oskil-Vovchansk east), Zaporizhzhia (Ukrainian north and post-2022 occupied south) and Kherson (liberated right bank and post-2022 occupied left bank) into 11 occupation-history zones, yielding 33 Ukrainian divisions in all.

Inside the Russian Federation, mobilisation and casualty patterns followed federal-subject boundaries just as closely. Presidential Decree No. 647 of 21 September 2022 (the "partial mobilisation" of over 300k reservists) assigned call-up quotas to each of the 83 federal subjects - 46 oblasts, 21 republics, 9 krais, 4 autonomous okrugs, 1 autonomous oblast and 2 federal cities - through regional military commissariats chaired by each governor [@bessudnov2022ethnic; @istories2024mobilisation]. From 2023 to 2026, volunteer contract recruitment (*kontraktniki*) relied on fiscal competition in governor-set regional sign-up bonuses, which ranged from 400k-800k roubles in poorer oblasts to 1,9M-3,2M roubles in Moscow City, Khanty-Mansi AO, Belgorod Oblast, Tatarstan, Bashkortostan, Sverdlovsk and Leningrad Oblast. Shelled western border oblasts (Belgorod, Kursk and Bryansk) raised local territorial defence units, while independent mortality monitors - Mediazona, BBC News Russian and Meduza/Kobak - track military fatalities by federal subject [@mediazona2025casualties; @meduza2024probate; @kobak2023excess].

s_json <- jsonlite::fromJSON((if (file.exists("russian_invasion_of_ukraine_summary.json")) "russian_invasion_of_ukraine_summary.json" else "../../_shared/_gis_cache/russian_invasion_of_ukraine_summary.json"))

colnames(pops_mat) <- c("Y2021", "Y2022", "Y2023", "Y2024", "Y2025", "Y2026")

clean_tbl_str <- function (x) {
  x <- gsub("([0-9]{4})AD\\b", "\\1", as.character(x), perl = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("([0-9]+,[1-9]+)0+(?![0-9])", "\\1", gsub("([0-9]+),0+(?![0-9])", "\\1", x, perl = TRUE), perl = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Sievierodonetsk", "Sievierodo-netsk", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Syevyerodonetskyi", "Syevyerodo-netskyi", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Kostiantynivka", "Kostianty-nivka", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("Dnipropetrovsk", "Dnipro-petrovsk", x, fixed = TRUE)
  return(x)
}

cat_labels <- c(

  ua_liberated_2022 = "UA 2022 Occupied & Liberated Oblast Zones (2)",
  ua_occupied_2022 = "UA Newly Occupied 2022-2026 Oblast Zones (4)",
  ua_ordlo_crimea_2014 = "UA Pre-2022 Occupied Donbas & Crimea (4)",
  ua_border_deocc = "UA Feb-Apr 2022 Defended Border Oblasts (4)",
  ua_idp_hub = "UA Central & Southern IDP Hub Oblasts & Kyiv (7)",
  ua_west_sanctuary = "UA Western & Northern Rear Oblasts (9)",
  by_staging_core = "Belarus Oblasts & Minsk City (7)",
  ru_border_bars = "RU Shelled Western Border Oblasts (3)",
  ru_smd_rear = "RU Southern Military District Rear Subjects (5)",
  ru_capitals = "RU Federal Capitals & Metro Oblasts (4)",
  ru_hydrocarbon = "RU Hydrocarbon High-Bonus Autonomous Okrugs (2)",
  ru_vpk_core = "RU Defence-Industrial & Core Oblasts/Krais (39)",
  ru_garrison_high = "RU High-Loss Garrison, Arctic & Pacific Subjects (11)",
  ru_ethnic_high = "RU Disproportionate-Loss Ethnic Republics (19)"
)

fmt_k <- function (v) {
  vapply(as.numeric(v), function (val) {
    if (is.na(val)) return("-")
    if (val >= 1000) {
      s <- formatC(val / 1000.0, format = "f", digits = 2L, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",")
      s <- sub("(,[0-9]*?[1-9])0+$", "\\1", s, perl = TRUE)
      s <- sub(",0+$", "", s, perl = TRUE)
      return(paste0(s, "M"))
    }
    s <- formatC(round(val), format = "d", big.mark = ".")
    return(paste0(s, "k"))
  }, character(1))
}
fmt_pct <- function (p21, p26) {
  ch <- (p26 - p21) / p21 * 100
  s <- sprintf("%+.1f%%", ch)
  sub(",0%$", "%", gsub(".", ",", s, fixed = TRUE))
}

rows_list <- list()
for (ck in names(cat_labels)) {
  idx <- which(regs_df$map_cat == ck)
  sv <- unname(colSums(pops_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE]))
  rows_list[[length(rows_list) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
    Tier = cat_labels[[ck]],
    Y2021 = fmt_k(sv[1]), Y2022 = fmt_k(sv[2]), Y2023 = fmt_k(sv[3]),
    Y2024 = fmt_k(sv[4]), Y2025 = fmt_k(sv[5]), Y2026 = fmt_k(sv[6]),
    Change = fmt_pct(sv[1], sv[6]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
  )
}
for (cn in c("Ukraine", "Belarus", "Russia")) {
  idx <- which(regs_df$country == cn)
  sv <- unname(colSums(pops_mat[idx, , drop = FALSE]))
  lbl <- if (cn == "Ukraine") "Ukraine Subtotal (33 Oblast & Occupation Units across 27 Oblasts)" else if (cn == "Belarus") "Belarus Subtotal (7 Oblasts & Minsk City)" else "Russian Federation Subtotal (83 Federal Subjects, 1991 Borders)"
  rows_list[[length(rows_list) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
    Tier = lbl,
    Y2021 = fmt_k(sv[1]), Y2022 = fmt_k(sv[2]), Y2023 = fmt_k(sv[3]),
    Y2024 = fmt_k(sv[4]), Y2025 = fmt_k(sv[5]), Y2026 = fmt_k(sv[6]),
    Change = fmt_pct(sv[1], sv[6]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
  )
}
sv_tot <- unname(colSums(pops_mat))
rows_list[[length(rows_list) + 1L]] <- data.frame(
  Tier = "Total Domain (All 123 Oblast, Occupation & Subject Units)",
  Y2021 = fmt_k(sv_tot[1]), Y2022 = fmt_k(sv_tot[2]), Y2023 = fmt_k(sv_tot[3]),
  Y2024 = fmt_k(sv_tot[4]), Y2025 = fmt_k(sv_tot[5]), Y2026 = fmt_k(sv_tot[6]),
  Change = fmt_pct(sv_tot[1], sv_tot[6]), stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
df_macro_sum <- do.call(rbind, rows_list)
rownames(df_macro_sum) <- NULL
render_table_template(
  df_macro_sum,

    caption = "Resident population by regional tier and national subtotal from 2021 to 2026.",
    col_names = c("Regional Tier (Units)", "2021", "2022", "2023", "2024", "2025", "2026", "Change"),
    label = "tab:macro-summary"

)

# Methodology

Because martial law in Ukraine suspended the planned 2023 All-Ukrainian Census and wartime censorship in the Russian Federation restricted granular Rosstat demographic tables after mid-2022 [@libanova2023ukraine; @raksha2023fertility; @meduza2024probate; @kobak2023excess], reconstructing regional population and settlement trajectories from 2021 to 2026 relies on seven complementary bodies of evidence.

## Conflict Events, Frontlines and Satellite Damage

Combat intensity and territorial control are tracked by pairing geo-located conflict logs with satellite imagery. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED) provides 138 Ukrainian raion polygons aggregating 5,89k high-intensity shelling and combat clusters and 16,3k baseline fatalities alongside more than 180k conflict events recorded through 2025-2026 [@acled2025ukraine; @attar2024linked]. Fifteen frontline raions across Donetsk, Luhansk, Kherson, Kharkiv and Kyiv Oblasts account for the bulk of urban wartime destruction (Table \ref{tab:acled-raions} and Figure \ref{fig:displacement-cascade}B). In parallel, DeepState frontline maps delineate the active line of contact and Russian-occupied shares inside Luhansk Oblast (~98% occupied), Donetsk Oblast (~70% occupied), Zaporizhzhia Oblast (~73% occupied), Kherson Oblast (~72% occupied left bank), Kharkiv Oblast (~3% border strip) and AR Crimea and Sevastopol (100% occupied since 2014), hatched in crimson over modern oblast borders in Figure \ref{fig:hero} [@deepstate2025map; @winkler2024high]. At the settlement level, building damage classifications derived from Copernicus Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) interferometric coherence, UNOSAT optical assessments and World Bank Rapid Damage and Needs Assessments (USD 524B in reconstruction needs across over 2,5M damaged housing units) are cross-checked against NASA/NOAA VIIRS night-time radiance series tracking urban depopulation and power-grid blackouts [@scher2023sar; @unosat2023mariupol; @worldbank2023rdna2; @worldbank2024rdna3; @worldbank2025rdna4; @minora2023ukraine; @aimi2023ukraine].

## Administrative Registries, Displacement and Mortality

For Kyiv-controlled territories, demographic estimates developed by the Ptoukha Institute for Demography and Social Studies (Ella Libanova, Oleksandr Gladun, Pavlo Shevchuk and Nataliia Levchuk) combine active mobile-operator SIM cards (Kyivstar, Vodafone Ukraine and lifecell), eHealth medical declarations, oblast IDP subsistence allowances, school enrolments and municipal water and bread consumption [@libanova2023ukraine; @libanova2024demographic; @gladun2023war; @gladun2024mortality; @shevchuk2023reconstruction; @ukraine2024strategy; @ukrstat2022chiselnist]. Cross-border refugee stocks (6,4M globally in 2026, including ~4,3M EU Temporary Protection beneficiaries) are anchored by UNHCR and Eurostat registers [@unhcr2025ukraine; @eurostat2025temporary; @mazzoli2023ukraine; @kim2023ukraine; @scherbov2024eastern], while oblast-level IDP (3,67M) and returnee (4,45M) figures are drawn from IOM General Population Survey Rounds 1 to 18+ [@iom2022gps; @iom2024displacement; @iom2025returns; @unocha2024ukraine; @leasure2022ukraine; @boy2023ukraine; @gonzalez2022ukraine].

Combat and civilian mortality estimates integrate the Mediazona and BBC News Russian named-obituary database (over 105k individually named Russian military dead by 2025-2026, coded by federal subject) with Meduza and Dmitry Kobak's probate-registry excess mortality model (160k-220k+ total Russian military dead) [@meduza2024probate; @kobak2023excess; @mediazona2025casualties; @bessudnov2022ethnic; @istories2024mobilisation], alongside UALosses (over 70k named Ukrainian military dead), UN OHCHR civilian casualty monitors (12,6k+ recorded killed, excluding the Mariupol siege toll of 22k-25k+) and satellite cemetery measurements [@ohchr2025casualties; @kovalenko2024ukraine; @stojkoski2023ukraine; @shevchenko2023mariupol; @ballinger2024battle; @dietrich2024ukraine; @dietrich2024mapping]. Wartime emigration from Russia (650k-1,05M at peak, with 580k-680k net retained abroad in 2026) and Belarus (200k-350k outflow) is quantified through receiving-state residence permits, tax identification numbers and banking registries across Poland, Lithuania, Germany, Kazakhstan, Armenia, Georgia, Serbia, Turkey, Israel and the UAE [@rerussia2024outflow; @kuznetsova2024russian; @wachs2022russian; @shcherbakova2024demographic; @dudin2023belarus].

# Results

## Ukrainian Oblasts and Occupation Zones

Within its internationally recognised 1991 borders, Ukraine's resident population fell by 6,21M (-14,2%) between 2021 and 2026, dropping from 43,87M before the full-scale invasion to 39,1M in 2022 and reaching 37,66M by early 2026. Of this 2026 population, roughly 31,4M reside in Kyiv-controlled territory and 6,2M live across Russian-occupied Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk and southern Zaporizhzhia and Kherson Oblasts [@libanova2024demographic; @iom2025returns; @unhcr2025ukraine]. Table \ref{tab:ukraine-oblasts} and Figure \ref{fig:displacement-cascade} set out the regional figures across all 33 divisions.

```{r fig-displacement-cascade, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_figure_template(
  "figures/russian_invasion_of_ukraine_fig2_population_trajectory.png",
  list(
    caption = "Comparison of 2021 and 2026 resident and displaced populations across Ukrainian oblasts alongside conflict intensity in the leading frontline raions.",
    label = "fig:displacement-cascade"
  )
)
```

### Frontline and Partially Occupied Oblasts

Ukraine's five frontline oblasts - Donetsk (UA-14), Luhansk (UA-09), Kharkiv (UA-63), Zaporizhzhia (UA-23) and Kherson (UA-65) - experienced severe depopulation, declining collectively from 11,44M in 2021 to 6,66M in 2026 (-41,8%). In Donetsk Oblast (4,06M to 2,14M, -47,3%; 109th Territorial Defence Brigade), the 2022 siege of Mariupol (432k to 195k, with 22k-25k+ civilian dead) [@shevchenko2023mariupol; @ballinger2024battle; @unosat2023mariupol], the near-total destruction of Bakhmut (71k to 0,3k), Avdiivka (31k to 0,7k), Toretsk (31k to 1,2k), Vuhledar (14k to 0,1k) and Kurakhove (18k to 0,9k) and mandatory evacuations from Pokrovsk (60k to 5,5k) and Myrnohrad (46k to 2,8k) halved the regional population, leaving Kramatorsk (147k to 75k) and Sloviansk (105k to 54k) as fortified administrative hubs [@acled2025ukraine; @deepstate2025map]. Neighbouring Luhansk Oblast (2,1M to 1,24M, -41%; 111th Brigade) fell almost entirely under Russian occupation following the 2022 assaults on Popasna (19k to 0,25k), Sievierodonetsk (101k to 18k) and Lysychansk (93k to 18k).

Further north, Kharkiv Oblast (2,62M to 1,84M, -29,8%; 113th and 127th Brigades) defended Kharkiv City (1,42M to 1,2M, hosting over 200k intra-oblast IDPs) and liberated Izium (45k to 23,5k) in September 2022, but renewed 2024-2025 border fighting forced the evacuation of Kupiansk (27k to 3,2k) and razed Vovchansk (17,5k to 0,15k) [@holoborodko2024kharkiv; @iom2025returns]. In the south, Zaporizhzhia Oblast (1,65M to 1,06M, -35,8%; 110th Brigade) remained divided between Ukrainian-held Zaporizhzhia City (710k to 530k, hosting ~210k IDPs) and Orikhiv (14k to 1,15k) and Russian-occupied Melitopol (149k to 110k), Berdiansk (106k to 74k) and Enerhodar (52k to 22k). Kherson Oblast (1,01M to 380k, -62,4%; 124th Brigade) suffered the steepest proportional loss of any Ukrainian region after the November 2022 liberation of right-bank Kherson City (279k to 66k), relentless cross-river shelling of Beryslav (12k to 1,2k) and the 6 June 2023 Kakhovka dam breach across Oleshky (24k to 8k) and Nova Kakhovka (45k to 13k) [@petrenko2024kakhovka; @unep2023kakhovka].

### De-Occupied Border Oblasts, Central Hubs and Western Sanctuaries

Across the four northern and southern border oblasts de-occupied in early 2022 - Mykolaiv (UA-48), Sumy (UA-59), Chernihiv (UA-74) and Kyiv Oblast (UA-32) - combined population declined by 14,1% from 4,93M to 4,24M. Rapid resistance by regular forces and Territorial Defence units between February and April 2022 repelled Russian advances on Mykolaiv (1,09M to 900k; 123rd Brigade), Chernihiv (975k to 755k; 119th Brigade), Sumy (1,03M to 795k; 117th Brigade) and Kyiv Oblast (1,83M to 1,78M; 114th Brigade). Whereas Kyiv Oblast (~245k IDPs) nearly recovered its pre-war population through rapid reconstruction in Bucha (37k to 38k) and Irpin (62k to 65k), Sumy and Chernihiv Oblasts lost over a fifth of their residents as cross-border shelling forced mandatory evacuations along the 5-15 km Russian frontier strip from 2023 to 2026 [@iom2025returns; @acled2025ukraine].

By contrast, Ukraine's seven central and southern IDP reception hubs - Kyiv City (UA-30), Dnipropetrovsk (UA-12), Odesa (UA-51), Poltava (UA-53), Cherkasy (UA-71), Kirovohrad (UA-35) and Vinnytsia (UA-05) - absorbed more than 1,6M displaced citizens, limiting their combined net contraction to 2,4% (13,42M to 13,1M). Anchored by Kyiv City (2,96M to 2,96M; 112th and 241st Brigades, ~375k IDPs) and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast (3,12M to 3,09M; 108th and 128th Brigades, Ukraine's largest IDP reception region with ~455k IDPs in Dnipro 968k to 980k and Kryvyi Rih 603k to 585k offsetting artillery evacuations from Nikopol 105k to 54k), IDP inflows kept population near pre-war parity in Poltava (1,36M to 1,37M, +0,7%; ~185k IDPs), Cherkasy (1,17M to 1,16M, -1,3%), Vinnytsia (1,52M to 1,47M, -3,6%), Kirovohrad (920k to 875k, -4,9%) and Odesa Oblast (2,37M to 2,18M, -8%) [@iom2025returns; @worldbank2025rdna4].

In the nine western and northern rear oblasts (11,64M to 11,3M, -2,9%), enterprise relocation and IDP settlement drove net wartime population growth in Zakarpattia (UA-21, 1,25M to 1,29M, +3,2%; 101st Brigade), Lviv (UA-46, 2,49M to 2,52M, +1,2%; 103rd and 125th Brigades, ~260k IDPs) and Chernivtsi (UA-77, 890k to 900k, +1,1%; 107th Brigade). Meanwhile, northern forest-belt oblasts - Volyn (UA-07, -7,7%), Rivne (UA-56, -8,6%) and Zhytomyr (UA-18, -10,9%) - alongside Ivano-Frankivsk (UA-26), Ternopil (UA-61) and Khmelnytskyi (UA-68), saw moderate contractions due to EU refugee departures and northern border fortification duty [@iom2025returns; @unhcr2025ukraine]. In Russian-occupied Crimea (UA-43 and UA-40, 2,44M to 2,36M, -3,3%), both the Autonomous Republic (1,93M to 1,88M) and Sevastopol City (510k to 485k) contracted under strikes on the Black Sea Fleet and Crimean Tatar draft flight.

## Belarus and Shelled Russian Border Oblasts

Separating Belarus into its seven administrative divisions (six oblasts plus Minsk City; Table \ref{tab:belarus-oblasts}) and isolating Russia's three shelled western border oblasts (RU-BEL, RU-KRS and RU-BRY) highlights frontier contractions that national totals obscure.

In February 2022, Russian forces launched the northern Kyiv and Chernihiv offensive from staging bases in Gomel Oblast (1,33M to 1,25M, -6%; Gomel, Mozyr and Zyabrovka) and airfields in Brest Oblast (1,34M to 1,28M, -4,1%; Luninets and Baranovichi) [@deepstate2025map]. Between 2021 and 2026, Belarus's population declined by 380k (-4,1%, from 9,35M to 8,97M), driven by steep natural decrease (-55k to -65k annually at a total fertility rate of 1,16) in Vitebsk (-6,2%) and Mogilev (-6,2%) Oblasts and the emigration of 200k-350k IT specialists, physicians and skilled workers from Minsk City (2,01M to 1,98M) and Grodno Oblast (1,02M to 965k, -5,4%) to Poland and Lithuania [@belstat2024chislennost; @dudin2023belarus; @eurostat2025temporary].

Along Russia's western frontier with Ukraine, Belgorod, Kursk and Bryansk Oblasts contracted collectively by 6,8% (3,81M to 3,55M). From 2023 to 2025, artillery and drone bombardment along the Kharkiv-Belgorod border forced civilian evacuations from Shebekino (39,6k to 24k) and Graivoron, reducing Belgorod Oblast from 1,54M to 1,45M (-6,2%) even as regional authorities raised local territorial defence battalions and hiked one-time contract bonuses to 3M roubles [@acled2025ukraine; @istories2024mobilisation]. In August 2024, Ukraine's cross-border incursion into Kursk Oblast (1,08M to 985k, -9%) captured Sudzha (5,1k to 0,6k) and displaced 130k-150k residents toward Kursk City (440k to 425k), Zheleznogorsk and Oryol, while Bryansk Oblast (1,19M to 1,12M, -5,7%) contracted under border shelling and natural decrease [@deepstate2025map; @rosstat2024demografiya].

## Mobilisation and Mortality in the Russian Federation

Across all 83 internationally recognised federal subjects of the Russian Federation (within 1991 borders, excluding occupied Ukrainian territories), the resident population declined by 2,93M (-2%), from 144,86M in 2021 to 141,93M in 2026 (Tables \ref{tab:ethnic-casualties} and \ref{tab:russia-subjects}; Figure \ref{fig:ethnic-casualties}). Because mobilisation quotas, governor sign-up bonuses, defence-industrial exemptions and permanent garrison deployments followed regional boundaries, wartime demographic trajectories diverged sharply across five federal-subject groups.

```{r fig-ethnic-casualties, echo=FALSE, results='asis'}
render_figure_template(
  "figures/russian_invasion_of_ukraine_fig3_subregional_distribution.png",
  list(
    caption = "Confirmed military fatalities per 10k working-age men across Russian federal subjects and estimated wartime emigration by destination country.",
    label = "fig:ethnic-casualties"
  )
)
```

### Metropolitan Capitals and High-Mortality Republics

To insulate metropolitan populations from political backlash, federal authorities kept compulsory mobilisation minimal in Moscow City (RU-MOS, 3,2 confirmed deaths per 10k working-age men; 13,01M to 12,88M in 2022 before rebounding to 13,12M in 2026) and Saint Petersburg (RU-SPE, 6,8 per 10k; 5,6M to 5,57M), alongside surrounding Moscow Oblast (RU-MOW) and Leningrad Oblast (RU-LEN). Both capitals relied on 1,9M-2,5M+ rouble contract bonuses to meet recruitment targets while generating over 65% of Russia's 650k-1,05M skilled wartime emigrants [@bessudnov2022ethnic; @rerussia2024outflow; @kuznetsova2024russian].

At the opposite extreme, Mediazona and BBC obituaries alongside Meduza and Kobak probate excess male mortality estimates reveal steep ethnic and rural stratification across Russia's 19 high-loss ethnic republics [@bessudnov2022ethnic; @meduza2024probate; @kobak2023excess; @mediazona2025casualties]. Per-capita confirmed mortality peaked in Tuva (RU-TY, 122 per 10k men, or 38,1x Moscow's rate; 55th Mountain Brigade in Kyzyl), Buryatia (RU-BU, 96 per 10k, 30x Moscow; 36th Combined Arms Army in Ulan-Ude and Kyakhta) and the Altai Republic (RU-AL, 82 per 10k, 25,6x Moscow). In the Volga-Ural and Caucasus belt, Bashkortostan (RU-BA, 4,09M to 4,01M) suffered the highest absolute military death toll of any Russian federal subject (over 4,85k named dead and 8,7k-10,5k+ total estimated dead; 44,5 per 10k), accompanied by heavy losses in North Ossetia-Alania (RU-SE, 56 per 10k), Kalmykia (RU-KL, 46), Mari El (RU-ME, 43,8), Chuvashia (RU-CU, 42,5), Udmurtia (RU-UD, 36,2), Sakha/Yakutia (RU-SA, 35), Dagestan (RU-DA, 29,5, where above-replacement fertility of ~1,95 still sustained net growth from 3,18M to 3,29M) and Tatarstan (RU-TA, 26,5, where 2M+ rouble bonuses and *Alga*/*Timer* battalion losses coincided with Kazan aviation and Alabuga drone manufacturing expansion) [@mediazona2025casualties; @istories2024mobilisation].

### Garrison Regions, Hydrocarbon Okrugs and the Industrial Core

Eleven northern, airborne and Pacific garrison subjects experienced severe combat attrition compounded by structural Far Eastern and Arctic out-migration. Permanent brigade home stations in Zabaykalsky Krai (RU-ZAB, 74 deaths per 10k; 29th CAA in Chita and Borzya), Sakhalin Oblast (RU-SAK, 62,5; 39th Brigade), Chukotka AO (RU-CHU, 58), Magadan Oblast (RU-MAG, 54), Pskov Oblast (RU-PSK, 49,5; 76th VDV Air Assault Division), Kamchatka Krai (RU-KAM, 48,5; 40th Naval Infantry), Murmansk Oblast (RU-MUR, 46,2; 200th Arctic Brigade) and Primorsky Krai (RU-PRI, 41,5; Vladivostok 155th Naval Infantry and Ussuriysk 5th CAA) suffered some of the highest non-republic casualty rates in the federation [@mediazona2025casualties; @rosstat2024demografiya].

Conversely, the two hydrocarbon autonomous okrugs - Khanty-Mansi (RU-KHM) and Yamalo-Nenets (RU-YAN) - offered record 2,75M-3,2M rouble regional sign-up bonuses in 2024-2025 to fulfil federal quotas via out-of-region recruits while shielding Surgut, Nizhnevartovsk and Novy Urengoy oil-and-gas shift crews, enabling slight net demographic growth (2,25M to 2,29M, +1,6%) [@istories2024mobilisation]. Across Russia's 44 defence-industrial and southern rear oblasts and krais, round-the-clock three-shift munitions, tank and aircraft production in Sverdlovsk (RU-SVE, Nizhny Tagil Uralvagonzavod), Chelyabinsk (RU-CHE), Perm (RU-PER), Tula (RU-TUL), Nizhny Novgorod (RU-NIZ), Samara (RU-SAM), Novosibirsk (RU-NVS), Omsk (RU-OMS), Krasnoyarsk (RU-KYA), Irkutsk (RU-IRK) and Khabarovsk (RU-KHA) stabilised core industrial cities even as rural districts and penal/contract cohorts absorbed heavy casualties (30-43 confirmed dead per 10k men), while Southern Military District rear hubs in Krasnodar Krai (RU-KDA, 5,84M to 5,93M) and Rostov Oblast (RU-ROS, 4,2M to 4,14M) anchored military logistics [@rosstat2024demografiya; @mediazona2025casualties].

## Fertility, Mortality and Labour Shocks

Beyond territorial displacement, the war reshaped vital rates, age-sex pyramids, disability prevalence and labour markets across all 123 administrative and occupation-history divisions (Figure \ref{fig:vital-shock} and Table \ref{tab:vital-rates}).

In Ukraine, total fertility collapsed from 1,16 (273,8k live births) in 2021 to 0,92 (206k) in 2022 and ~0,77-0,82 across 2023-2026 (falling to ~170k births per year by 2025-2026), driven by the wartime separation of roughly 1M mobilised men from 2,8M reproductive-age women displaced abroad [@libanova2024demographic; @gladun2024mortality; @levchuk2023fertility; @eurostat2025temporary]. With annual deaths (~515k) running at three times annual births, Ukraine's natural population balance fell to -345k per year alongside 50k-70k+ war amputees and more than 300k conflict-disabled citizens [@worldbank2025rdna4; @ohchr2025casualties].

In the Russian Federation, following roughly 1,05M excess COVID-19 deaths across 2020-2022 [@kobak2021regional], annual live births dropped from 1,4M (TFR 1,5) in 2021 to 1,22M (TFR 1,39) in 2025-2026 - the smallest birth cohort since 1999 [@rosstat2024demografiya; @raksha2023fertility; @zakharov2023fertility; @shcherbakova2024demographic]. Combined with 160k-220k+ military dead, 320k-450k severely wounded (+290k working-age male disability pensioners in Social Fund registers) and over 580k net emigrants, Russia lost 1,8M-2,2M civilian male workers, pushing official unemployment down to 2,3%-2,6% amid acute industrial wage inflation [@meduza2024probate; @rerussia2024outflow].

# Conclusion

Between 2021 and 2026, the Russo-Ukrainian War reduced the combined resident population of Ukraine, Belarus and the Russian Federation by 9,52M, from 198,08M to 188,56M. In Ukraine, a net contraction of 6,21M (-14,2%) shifted the country's demographic centre of gravity westward and inward: frontline oblasts across the Donbas and the lower Dnieper lost more than two-fifths of their pre-war inhabitants to siege destruction, occupation and evacuation, whereas Kyiv, Dnipropetrovsk and the western oblasts absorbed millions of displaced citizens. In Belarus (-380k) and the Russian Federation (-2,93M), wartime losses compounded pre-existing natural decrease with working-age emigration and steep regional disparities in military mortality, which fell hardest on peripheral ethnic republics and garrison oblasts while largely sparing Moscow and Saint Petersburg.

  Y2026 = fmt_k(pops_mat[ru_idx, 6]),
  Change = mapply(fmt_pct, pops_mat[ru_idx, 1], pops_mat[ru_idx, 6]),
  Mort = paste0(sub(",0$", "", gsub("\\.", ",", as.character(regs_df$deaths_per_10k[ru_idx]))), "/10k"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
)
ru_tot <- unname(colSums(pops_mat[ru_idx, , drop = FALSE]))
df_ru <- rbind(df_ru, data.frame(
  Subject = "Russian Federation Total (All 83 Federal Subjects)",
  Y2021 = fmt_k(ru_tot[1]), Y2022 = fmt_k(ru_tot[2]), Y2023 = fmt_k(ru_tot[3]),
  Y2024 = fmt_k(ru_tot[4]), Y2025 = fmt_k(ru_tot[5]), Y2026 = fmt_k(ru_tot[6]),
  Change = fmt_pct(ru_tot[1], ru_tot[6]),
  Mort = "~28,5/10k",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE, row.names = NULL
))
rownames(df_ru) <- NULL
render_table_template(
  df_ru,
  list(
    caption = "Resident population and confirmed military deaths per 10k working-age men across all 83 federal subjects of the Russian Federation from 2021 to 2026.",
    col_names = c("Federal Subject (ISO)", "2021", "2022", "2023", "2024", "2025", "2026", "Change", "Deaths/10k"),
    label = "tab:russia-subjects"
  )
)
